lessons.title: Case Study: Backtesting a Bollinger Band Strategy on a Nifty Stock in Python

children.text: This chapter built three separate signal generators, Bollinger Bands, RSI, and moving-average reversion. A signal is not a strategy until you attach a precise entry rule, a precise exit rule, a stop-loss, and a position size to it, and then run the whole thing over history to see what actually happens. This case study builds that complete loop, end to end, using the Bollinger Band strategy from Lesson 9 on a hypothetical NSE midcap, Delta Industries.

body.text: A backtest is only as trustworthy as its honesty about what information was actually available at each point in time. The single most common way a backtest lies to you is by letting a trade fill at a price the strategy could not have known about when the signal fired. Everything else in this case study is secondary to getting that one detail right.

Close back at or above the middle band

markDefs.definition: A backtesting error where a simulated trade uses information that would not actually have been available at the moment the trade was placed, typically by filling at a price the signal itself was calculated from.

children.text: A tempting but flawed backtest buys at the same day's closing price that triggered the signal, since that close is already sitting in the dataframe. In live trading, you only learn a day's closing price after the market has shut for the day. There is no way to also transact at that same price at that same moment. This is

, and it is one of the most common ways an amateur backtest quietly overstates its own returns. Chapter 7 covers the full family of backtesting traps. This case study fixes the most basic one directly: every entry fills at the next trading day's opening price, not the close that generated the signal.

body.code:
import pandas as pd

window, k = 20, 2
stop_loss_pct = -0.05
max_hold_days = 10

df = pd.DataFrame({"close": close, "open": open_})
df["ma"] = df["close"].rolling(window).mean()
df["std"] = df["close"].rolling(window).std()
df["lower"] = df["ma"] - k * df["std"]

trades = []
in_trade = False

for i in range(window, len(df) - 1):
    if not in_trade and df["close"].iloc[i] < df["lower"].iloc[i]:
        entry_price = df["open"].iloc[i + 1]   # next day's open, no look-ahead
        entry_idx = i + 1
        in_trade = True
        continue

    if in_trade:
        days_held = i - entry_idx
        ret = (df["close"].iloc[i] - entry_price) / entry_price
        hit_target = df["close"].iloc[i] >= df["ma"].iloc[i]
        hit_stop = ret <= stop_loss_pct
        timed_out = days_held >= max_hold_days

        if hit_target or hit_stop or timed_out:
            trades.append({
                "entry_price": round(entry_price, 2),
                "exit_price": round(df["close"].iloc[i], 2),
                "return_pct": round(ret * 100, 2),
                "days_held": days_held,
                "reason": "target" if hit_target else "stop" if hit_stop else "timeout",
            })
            in_trade = False

results = pd.DataFrame(trades)
print(results)
print(f"Win rate: {(results['return_pct'] > 0).mean():.1%}")
print(f"Average return per trade: {results['return_pct'].mean():.2f}%")
body.caption: A minimal, honest backtest loop: signal on close, fill on next open, exit on target, stop, or timeout, whichever comes first.

children.text: What the Backtest Actually Tells You (and What It Doesn't)

Eight trades is nowhere near enough to draw a confident conclusion about whether this rule has a real edge. A 62.5% win rate on eight trades could easily be six or seven coin flips going your way, not a repeatable pattern. Treat a small backtest like this one as a sanity check on the mechanics, not as proof of profitability. This version also deliberately leaves out several real costs that a serious evaluation cannot skip: brokerage and Securities Transaction Tax on every entry and exit, the bid-ask spread and market impact of actually buying a midcap stock that just fell sharply, and the fact that Delta Industries' own theta and phi, estimated from Chapter 2's tools, may have shifted since this backtest window, since parameters are estimates, not constants.

body.text: A 1.19% average return per trade sounds fine until you subtract real costs. Round-trip brokerage on a discount broker is small, but Securities Transaction Tax on equity delivery, exchange charges, and the slippage from buying a stock that just gapped down on a thin order book can easily eat one-third to one-half of an edge this size on a midcap name. A strategy that looks profitable before costs can be a break-even or losing strategy after them. Chapter 7 covers transaction costs and slippage as a dedicated topic, not an afterthought.

body.title: Compute the win rate
body.prompt: A different backtest produced 10 trades with these percentage returns: +4, +2, -3, +5, -6, +1, +3, -2, +4, -5. What was the win rate, as a percentage?
body.explanation: Six of the ten trades were positive (+4, +2, +5, +1, +3, +4), and four were negative. 6 out of 10 is a 60% win rate.

body.title: Spot the backtesting error
body.question: A trader backtests a Bollinger Band strategy by buying at a stock's closing price on the same day that closing price is used to calculate whether it fell below the lower band. What is wrong with this backtest?
options: Nothing, this is exactly how the strategy would work in live trading
It fills the trade at a price that would not actually have been known and tradeable at the moment the signal fired, a form of look-ahead bias
The lower band should have used a 50-day window instead of 20
Win rate cannot be calculated unless the stop-loss is removed
body.explanation: You only know a day's closing price after the exchange has closed for the day, at which point you cannot also transact at that same closing price. Filling the simulated trade at that same close is look-ahead bias: it assumes access to a price the strategy could not actually have acted on in real time. The fix, used throughout this case study, is filling at the next trading day's open instead.

points: A backtest requires a complete, precisely defined rule set: entry signal, entry fill price, target exit, stop-loss, a time-based exit, and a position size, not just a signal.

The most basic backtesting error is filling a trade at a price the strategy could not have known when the signal fired. Fill on the next available price, never on the same close that generated the signal.
A small number of backtested trades, like the eight in this case study, is a sanity check on mechanics, not proof of a real, repeatable edge.

Transaction costs, Securities Transaction Tax, and slippage are not an afterthought. A strategy with a thin average edge per trade can be unprofitable after real Indian market costs, even if it looks solid on paper.
This closes Chapter 3. Chapter 4 moves from price reversion to volatility reversion, applying the same statistical instincts to how India VIX itself tends to behave after a spike.
